strengths: Well-motivated application problem: Identifies genuine gap between artificial perturbations in standard GCL and realistic biological perturbations in gene knockdown experiments
Principled probabilistic framework: Sound formulation using KL divergence with correct theoretical decomposition (Theorem 1) and elegant connection to standard GCL as limiting case (Corollary 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 13 downstream tasks across 3 cancer types with proper cross-validation, relevant baselines, and real public datasets (TCGA, LINCS)
Strong reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters (Table 8), clear algorithm description, comprehensive appendices, and promise to release code
Effective visualization: t-SNE and PCA analysis demonstrates SupGCL learns better graph-level structure, particularly for disease subtype separation
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: Core contribution is data-driven (using knockdown supervision) rather than technical. Framework applies standard KL divergence decomposition without new learning techniques or theoretical insights

Modest empirical improvements with unclear statistical significance: Many gains fall within standard deviation ranges; paper acknowledges lack of statistical significance in some tasks; no formal significance testing or multiple comparison corrections applied

Severe practical limitations: Method requires teacher GRNs from same cancer type—explicitly acknowledged limitation restricting real-world applicability. Authors' future work on cross-cancer models suggests fundamental constraint
Weak node-level results: Figure 3 shows no clear biological process clustering across any method; node embeddings remain dispersed suggesting limited success in learning node-level biological meaning
Unexplained computational overhead: SupGCL requires 2-3× training time (21.4 hours vs 3.4-10.8 hours) with no analysis of cause or justification provided

Incomplete ablation studies: No systematic investigation of temperature parameter sensitivity, no ablation isolating node-level vs augmentation-level loss contributions, cannot determine which components drive improvements

Unaddressed data quality concerns: GRN estimation is uncertain; batch effects between TCGA and LINCS platforms not discussed; only 768-948 of 975 genes have knockdown data—impact of coverage gaps unexplored

Lack of biological validation: No expert review or comparison with known regulatory relationships; Gene Ontology labels used only as downstream task targets; cannot confirm biologically meaningful learning beyond task performance
Limited generalization analysis: Experiments restricted to cancer GRNs; no sensitivity analysis for amount/quality of knockdown data; unclear if approach transfers beyond domain-specific setting
Theoretical contributions modest: Theorem 1 applies standard KL divergence decomposition without convergence guarantees, sample complexity analysis, or new theoretical insights

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Identifies genuine limitation that artificial perturbations in standard GCL misalign with biological reality in gene regulatory networks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Evaluates on 13 downstream tasks across 3 cancer types with both node-level and graph-level objectives
Consistent empirical improvements: Shows performance gains across all tested tasks and datasets
Thorough experimental reporting: Includes detailed hyperparameters, supplementary analyses, latent space visualizations, and ablations on embedding dimensions
Clear presentation: Paper is well-written with clear motivation and method explanation
weaknesses: CRITICAL: Unfair experimental comparison - SupGCL uses supervision information (teacher GRNs) that baseline methods lack access to. Improvements could reflect additional training signal rather than methodological superiority. Missing ablation: no comparison of SupGCL with/without teacher GRNs or baselines given equivalent supervision access

Weak theoretical contribution - Theorem 1 is straightforward application of textbook KL divergence decomposition. Corollary 1 (recovering standard GCL when τ_a→∞) is unsurprising behavior of temperature parameters. Claims of theoretical novelty are not supported

Severe applicability limitations - Method requires gene knockdown data for exact same genes and cancer types being studied. Paper acknowledges but inadequately emphasizes this constraint. No cross-cancer-type generalization experiments. Future work still needs to solve this limitation, indicating it is unresolved

Statistical significance unclear - No significance testing provided despite having standard deviations. Many results show overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Table 2 BP/Breast: 0.243±0.052 vs 0.230±0.051). Claims of 'consistent outperformance' lack quantitative validation

Representation quality not validated - Figure 3 admits 'no clear clustering observed based on labels' for node-level embeddings. If method learns better representations, why don't biological process labels show improved separation? Latent space visualizations don't demonstrate clear quality improvements

Critical missing ablations - No ablation isolating contribution of supervised signal (SupGCL ±teacher GRNs). No fair baseline comparison where other methods receive equivalent knockdown supervision. No robustness analysis for noisy/imperfect teacher networks. Temperature parameter claims unvalidated

Data leakage and confounding - TCGA patient data evaluated using LINCS cell line supervision. Both share 975 genes and cancer types. Knockdown patterns from cell lines could transfer trivially to patient classification without learning meaningful GRN structure
Computational overhead not justified - SupGCL requires ~21.4 hours vs 10.77 (GRACE), 8.3 (GraphCL) hours—2-3× slower—but trade-off not discussed or justified in paper
Limited domain coverage - All experiments on cancer GRNs. Generalization to other biological systems unexplored. Critical limitation (same-cancer-type requirement) only mentioned in conclusion

GRN construction not validated - Uses Bayesian network estimation with specific hyperparameters but no sensitivity analysis. Network quality directly affects all downstream results but robustness unexplored

strengths: Well-motivated problem: clearly identifies a genuine limitation in applying standard GCL to biological networks where artificial perturbations lack biological realism, motivating use of actual gene knockdown data

Sound theoretical framework: Theorem 1 provides principled probabilistic formulation showing GCL as special case via standard KL decomposition; Corollary 1 demonstrates theoretical connection to conventional methods

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: 13 downstream tasks across 3 cancer types with real biological data (TCGA/LINCS), 5 baseline comparisons, multiple metrics, and extensive supplementary analyses with ablations
Consistent improvements across all tasks and datasets demonstrated through well-organized results tables and latent space visualizations showing SupGCL's superior subtype separation

Strong reproducibility: extensive experimental details in appendices (preprocessing pipeline, hyperparameter settings documented in Tables 6-9, computational resources specified, algorithm pseudocode provided)
Thoughtful additional analyses: PCA analysis revealing GraphCL's latent space collapse, embedding dimension ablations, and latent space visualizations providing insights beyond primary metrics
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: core contribution is substituting supervised embeddings into existing GCL framework; Theorem 1 applies standard KL decomposition without fundamental new insight

Modest empirical improvements with questionable statistical significance: many improvements fall within overlapping error bars (e.g., BP Breast 0.243±0.052 vs GRACE 0.230±0.051); paper acknowledges lack of statistical significance in multiple tasks; no formal significance testing provided

Critical practical limitation severely restricting generalizability: method requires aligned knockdown experiments for each cancer type, limiting real-world applicability; essentially requires new experimental data for each new domain

Insufficient ablation studies: no comparison of Frobenius inner product with alternatives; limited temperature parameter sensitivity analysis; missing component importance ablations (Loss_Aug vs Loss_node)

Questionable biological assumptions: independence assumption p_φ(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p_φ(a,b) not justified; unclear why artificial masking should produce embeddings similar to biological knockdown; assumption that knockdown perturbations guide patient-level learning lacks justification

Compounded uncertainty from network estimation: both patient GRNs and teacher GRNs estimated via sampling-based Bayesian networks; no error propagation analysis or validation of GRN accuracy; potential for cascading errors unexplored

Experimental rigor concerns: large standard deviations unexplained; baseline methods potentially not optimized for biological graphs; no formal statistical significance testing despite claiming consistent improvements; missing negative results or failure analysis
Incomplete code availability: implementation statement truncates mid-sentence without providing actual repository link, compromising reproducibility claims
Significant computational overhead not justified: SupGCL requires 2-3× longer training time than baselines (21.4 hr vs 3-11 hr) without analysis of whether improvements warrant this cost

Limited scope and generalization: only three cancer types tested; unclear generalization beyond oncology; node-level representations still lack clear functional clustering despite graph-level improvements

strengths: Novel and well-motivated idea leveraging real biological perturbations from knockdown experiments as supervision, challenging the trend toward augmentation-free methods
Sound theoretical framework with Theorem 1 elegantly showing existing GCL methods as special cases, and Corollary 1 proving standard GCL emerges as τ_a→∞
Comprehensive evaluation across 13 downstream tasks spanning 3 cancer types with multiple metrics (accuracy, C-index, F1, Jaccard index) and strong supplementary material
Excellent biological validation through GO/KEGG enrichment analysis (Appendix I) demonstrating learned representations capture meaningful biological modules
Demonstrated robustness to limited supervision (Table 20: maintains performance with 1/4 knockdown samples) and GRN estimation uncertainty (Table 21: robust across thresholds)
Consistent improvements across all evaluated settings despite modest magnitude, with clear latent space analysis showing better separation of disease subtypes
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements with limited statistical significance: many gains fall within error bars (Tables 2-3), and Table 15 shows significance in only a subset of tasks; marginal improvement on hazard prediction (0.650 vs 0.642) doesn't justify 2-4x computational cost

Critical limitation in cross-domain generalization: models fail when applied to different cancer types (Table 18 OOD: c-index drops to 0.603/0.583), severely limiting practical utility and suggesting overfitting to cancer-type-specific patterns
Limited technical novelty: core contribution is applying existing GCL frameworks with real supervision rather than developing fundamentally new techniques; Theorem 1 is standard KL decomposition

Significant computational overhead not adequately addressed: SupGCL requires 21.4 hrs (breast) vs 10.8 hrs (GRACE), a 2-4x increase relegated to appendix with no justification relative to modest improvements

Incomplete experimental comparisons: missing supervised variants of other GCL methods, no baseline with direct knockdown similarity, limited comparison with augmentation-adjustment methods (only Appendix F.5)
Domain shift between sources not discussed: teacher GRNs from cell lines (LINCS) applied to patient GRNs (TCGA), and cross-cancer-type failure suggests this mismatch is problematic

Hyperparameter sensitivity inadequately explored: Table 4 shows non-trivial variation with τ_a (c-index 0.670→0.656); no ablation on τ_n or relative weighting of loss terms; τ_a=0.25 selection appears arbitrary
Independence assumption never empirically validated: Theorem 1 assumes p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b) but correlation between node identity and augmentation type not measured
Limited scope and generalization evidence: restricted to 975 genes, 3 cancer types, each requiring dedicated knockdown dataset; unclear applicability to less-studied diseases or other domains
Importance sampling approximation quality not analyzed: Algorithm 1 uses approximation for normalization constants without discussing impact on convergence or accuracy

strengths: Well-motivated insight that biological perturbations should be exploited as supervision signals rather than avoided, with thoughtful critique of augmentation-free methods
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 13 downstream tasks and 3 cancer types with extensive supplementary material including ablations, cross-domain studies, and enrichment analyses
Elegant theoretical formulation (Theorem 1) showing conventional GCL as a special case and providing probabilistic interpretation
Real-world evaluation using TCGA and LINCS data on clinically relevant tasks (patient survival prediction, disease subtype classification)
Robust empirical performance across all evaluated tasks with consistent if modest improvements over baselines
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is straightforward application of existing contrastive learning with different supervision source; Theorem 1 uses standard KL divergence decomposition without significant new insights

Modest empirical improvements with limited statistical significance: many results have overlapping error bars (e.g., Hazard: 0.650±0.059 vs GRACE 0.642±0.064), and Table 15 shows significant improvements in only 4/13 tasks

Critical generalization limitation severely restricts impact: SupGCL fails to improve performance when trained on one cancer type and applied to another (Appendix G), contradicting claims of general-purpose representation learning

Confounded experimental design: pre-training uses TCGA patient GRNs while supervision comes from LINCS knockdowns; advantages may derive from additional supervision data rather than the method; missing comparison with direct supervised learning

Questionable theoretical assumptions: independence assumption in Theorem 1 (p(i,j,a,b) = p(i,j)p(a,b)) is stated but not justified—knockdowns inherently affect node-level biology, contradicting independence claim
Incomplete baseline comparisons: GRN-specific method MuSe-GNN not compared; augmentation-correction methods relegated to appendix; no direct supervised learning baseline
Unclear mechanisms of improvement: paper does not explain when or why SupGCL outperforms baselines or provide guidance for method applicability
Computational overhead not addressed: SupGCL requires 2× training time (21.40 hr vs 10.77 hr for GRACE) with modest performance gains, raising cost-benefit concerns
Limited biological validation: enrichment analysis only for breast cancer; claims about cancer-specific pathways somewhat hand-wavy; no experimental validation of predictions
Incomplete supervision: only 768/975 genes have knockdown data; impact of coverage gaps and biological realism of feature-zeroing knockdown model not thoroughly investigated

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: leveraging real biological perturbations from knockdown experiments as supervision for augmentation selection, rather than viewing structural changes as artifacts to avoid
Solid theoretical framework with Theorem 1 elegantly decomposing the loss into node-level and augmentation-level components; Corollary 1 shows conventional GCL as a special case

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 13 downstream tasks on 3 cancer types with extensive supplementary analyses including robustness studies, cross-domain evaluation, and biological enrichment analyses
Strong reproducibility: detailed appendices with hyperparameters, algorithm pseudocode, GRN estimation procedures, and public datasets used throughout
Biologically grounded: Latent space analysis demonstrates superior capture of functional gene modules (GO/KEGG enrichment) compared to baselines
weaknesses: Marginal and inconsistently significant empirical improvements: gains often within standard deviation ranges; statistical significance testing (Table 15) shows improvements on only 4/13 tasks; paper acknowledges lack of consistent statistical superiority

Critical generalization failure across cancer types: models fine-tuned on one cancer type show catastrophic performance drops on others (e.g., Breast→Lung: 0.163 vs 0.282 in-domain, 42% relative decline); this fundamentally limits practical applicability and is inadequately addressed

High data requirements limiting applicability: requires knockdown experiments for target genes (only 78-97% coverage available); performance sensitive to supervision data reduction; large computational costs for GRN estimation

Questionable modeling assumptions: knockdown representation (zeroing node/edge features) is simplistic; Theorem 1's independence assumption p(i,j,a,b)=p(i,j)p(a,b) lacks justification; Frobenius similarity choice unmotivated
Limited baseline comparisons: focuses on standard GCL methods; missing comparisons with other supervised or semi-supervised approaches; GCLink comparison only on link prediction with modified variant

Teacher GRN quality never validated: knockdown networks treated as ground truth without benchmarking against known biological networks; GRN estimation introduces sampling variability inadequately analyzed

Key ablation studies relegated to appendix: Table 4 on temperature parameter should be in main paper; no ablations separating component contributions; presentation obscures which aspects drive improvements
